entry: Inorganic compound, Na₂CO₃, also known as washing soda, soda ash or sal soda. It is a white, odorless, water-soluble salt that yields alkaline solutions. Historically extracted from the ashes of sodium-rich plants, it is now produced in large quantities from [[Sodium chloride]] and [[Limestone]] by the Solvay process, or by carbonating [[Sodium hydroxide]]. Its largest use is in glassmaking, where it acts as a flux for [[Silicon dioxide|silica]] and lowers the melting point of the mixture; about 50% of global use goes to glass manufacturing. It also lowers water hardness and is used in making [[Soap]], [[Paper]] and sodium compounds such as [[Borax|borax]], and it is a component of many dry soap powders.

Ionic compound, NaCl, with a 1:1 ratio of sodium and chloride ions. It occurs as the mineral halite and as transparent or translucent, brittle, hygroscopic crystals. As common table salt, it is used as a condiment and food preservative. Chemical production consumes most of the world's output, about 250 million tonnes a year in 2008. It is the starting point of the chloralkali process, which yields [[Chlorine]] and [[Sodium hydroxide]], and of the Solvay process, which makes [[Sodium carbonate]]. Its other major use is de-icing roadways in sub-freezing weather, and it is also used in textile dyeing and pulp and paper manufacturing.

Chemical element, symbol Na, with atomic number 11. A soft, silvery-white, highly reactive [[Alkali metal]] in group 1 of the periodic table, it does not occur free in nature and is found in minerals such as [[Feldspar|feldspars]] and halite. It is the sixth most abundant element in the Earth's crust, and sodium and chlorine are the most common dissolved elements by weight in the oceans. [[Humphry Davy]] first isolated it in 1807 by electrolysis of [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium hydroxide]]. Its only stable isotope is ²³Na. Sodium is essential to all animals and some plants: its ions are the major cation of extracellular fluid, and nerve impulses depend on their sudden flow into cells. Animal cells keep sodium concentrations roughly tenfold higher outside than inside by means of the [[Potassium|sodium–potassium]] pump.

Inorganic compound, NaOH, also known as caustic soda and lye. It is a white, ionic solid, highly soluble in water, releasing considerable heat when it dissolves, and it absorbs moisture and carbon dioxide from the air. A highly corrosive [[Base (chemistry)|base]] that decomposes lipids and proteins at ambient temperatures, it can cause severe chemical burns at high concentrations. It is used in making [[Paper]], wood pulp, textiles, drinking water, soaps and detergents, and as a drain cleaner. Its pure form melts at 318 °C. Worldwide production was about 83 million tons in 2022. Because it is one of the simplest hydroxides, it is often used with water and [[Hydrochloric acid]] to demonstrate the [[PH|pH]] scale to chemistry students.

Alkaline inorganic compound, NaOCl, the sodium salt of [[Hypochlorous acid]]. Its dilute aqueous solution, known as [[Bleach|chlorine bleach]], has been used as a disinfectant and bleaching agent since the 18th century and remains the most important chlorine-based bleach. The anhydrous compound is unstable and may decompose explosively, but its pentahydrate is stable if refrigerated. Mixing bleach with acids, such as limescale removers, releases toxic [[Chlorine]] gas. A common misconception holds that bleach and [[Ammonia|ammonia]] release chlorine; they instead form toxic chloramines, such as nitrogen trichloride.

Inorganic salt, NaNO₃, also known as Chile saltpeter. It is a white, deliquescent solid, very soluble in water, and a readily available source of the nitrate anion. It is used in [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], pyrotechnics, explosives, glass and pottery enamels, meat preservatives, and solid rocket propellant. The largest natural deposits are in [[Chile]] and Peru, where caliche ore was mined; for more than a century almost all of the world supply came from the [[Atacama Desert]] in northern Chile. After the [[War of the Pacific]] (1879–1884), Chile took over the richest deposits of Peru and Bolivia. With the onset of [[World War I]], Germany made synthetic saltpeter from ammonia produced by the [[Haber process]], developed by [[Fritz Haber]] and Carl Bosch, and by the 1940s demand for natural sodium nitrate had fallen sharply.

Inorganic compound, NaNO₂, the most important industrial nitrite salt. It is a white to slightly yellowish, hygroscopic, water-soluble powder. Its main industrial use is converting [[Amine|amines]] into diazo compounds, precursors to many dyes, and it is also a precursor to pharmaceuticals and pesticides. It is probably best known as a food additive in processed meats, where it speeds curing, inhibits Clostridium botulinum and gives cured meat its pink color. Its safety record is disputed because of possible carcinogenic effects. Known as E250, it is approved in the European Union, United States, and Australia and New Zealand.

Generic name for compounds of sodium oxide and [[Silicon dioxide|silica]] of variable composition, most of which dissolve readily in water. The chief member is sodium metasilicate, also called waterglass or liquid glass. The commercial product is often greenish or blue owing to iron-containing impurities. Its uses include [[Cement|cements]], coatings, passive fire protection, textile and lumber processing, refractory ceramics and [[Adhesive|adhesives]]. Commercial grades are classified by their SiO₂:Na₂O weight ratio, which ranges from 1:2 to 3.75:1. Solutions can be produced by heating quartz sand, [[Sodium hydroxide|caustic soda]] and water with steam. Heating to drive off water yields a hard silica gel used as a desiccant. Main applications are in detergents, paper deinking, water treatment and construction materials.

Inorganic compound, Na₂SO₄, and several related hydrates, all white solids highly soluble in water. Annual production is about 6 million tonnes, with the decahydrate a major commodity chemical. It is mainly used as a filler in powdered home laundry detergents and in the Kraft process of paper pulping. The decahydrate, known as Glauber's salt, was discovered in Austrian spring water in 1625 by Johann Rudolf Glauber, who used it as a laxative. In the 18th century it became a raw material for [[Sodium carbonate|soda ash]]; in the 19th century the Leblanc process, which used it as an intermediate, became the principal method of soda-ash production. Its solubility rises more than tenfold between 0 °C and 32.384 °C, where it peaks at 49.7 g/100 mL.

Two cities destroyed by God for their wickedness, according to Genesis. Lot, [[Abraham|Abraham's]] nephew, was spared with his daughters, while his wife became a pillar of salt for looking back. The cities appear in the [[Hebrew Bible]], the [[New Testament]] and the [[Quran]] as symbols of wickedness. Scholars debate the sins involved, which have been linked to sexual immorality, violence, arrogance and inhospitality. [[Judaism]] often stresses cruelty and inhospitality, while [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]] debate sexual and violent sins. Possible sites along the [[Dead Sea]], such as Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira, have been proposed, but archaeological evidence is inconclusive.

Capital and largest city of [[Bulgaria]], at the foot of Vitosha mountain in the western part of the country. Known as Serdica in antiquity, it was conquered by the [[Roman Republic]] in 29 BC and was incorporated into the [[First Bulgarian Empire]] by Khan Krum in 809. Conquered by the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]] in 1382, it was regional capital of the Rumelia Eyalet from 1530 to 1836. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878, and the city was selected as capital of the Third Bulgarian State the following year, beginning a period of intense demographic and economic growth. It is the 14th-largest city in the [[European Union]]. Three temples of [[Christianity]], [[Islam]] and [[Judaism]] stand close together, forming a "triangle of religious tolerance". Boyana Church was included on the World Heritage List in 1979. The city has about 1.28 million residents within 500 sq km.

American filmmaker and former actress, daughter of [[Francis Ford Coppola]]. She made her acting debut as an infant in *The Godfather* (1972) and later played Mary Corleone in *The Godfather Part III* (1990). Her directorial debut, *The Virgin Suicides* (1999), was the first of several films with actress Kirsten Dunst. She won the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay for *Lost in Translation* (2003) and was nominated for Best Director, becoming the third woman so nominated. Later films include *Marie Antoinette* (2006), *Somewhere* (2010) and *Priscilla* (2023). Her [[Netflix]] special *A Very Murray Christmas* (2015) earned a Primetime Emmy nomination.

Japanese multinational investment holding company headquartered in Minato, Tokyo, investing mainly in [[Technology|technology]]. Founded in 1981 as a software distributor by Masayoshi Son, its largest shareholder. Its Vision Fund, with over $100 billion in capital at its onset, is the world's largest technology-focused venture capital fund, with sovereign wealth investors from the [[Middle East]]. Holdings include stakes in Arm, Alibaba, WeWork and Deutsche Telekom. Its affiliate SoftBank Corporation is the third-largest wireless carrier in [[Japan]]. In 2025 the company announced, with OpenAI, MGX and Oracle, the Stargate [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] infrastructure project, estimated to cost $500 billion over four years.

Sweetened, usually carbonated, non-alcoholic drink. Its sweetener may be [[Sugar|sugar]], high-fructose corn syrup, fruit juice or a sugar substitute, and it may contain [[Caffeine]] and colorings. In many countries a drink must contain less than 0.5% alcohol by volume to be classed as a soft drink. Carbonated water was invented by [[Joseph Priestley]] in 1767, and in 1783 J. J. Schweppe formed Schweppes, which sold the world's first bottled soft drink. Brands founded in the 19th century include Dr Pepper (1885) and [[Coca-Cola]] (1886); later brands include [[Pepsi]]. The global market was valued at about $629 billion in 2024. Studies associate regular consumption of sugar-sweetened varieties with weight gain, [[Obesity]] and type 2 diabetes, prompting regulatory scrutiny, sugar taxes and reformulation.

Bat-and-ball [[Sport|sport]] between two teams on a diamond-shaped field, where teams take turns batting and fielding. It resembles [[Baseball]] but uses a larger ball on a smaller field, and games typically last seven innings. In fast-pitch, played at the high school, collegiate and professional levels, pitchers throw the ball underhand with a windmill motion at up to 78 miles per hour (124 km/h). Slow-pitch is common in recreational leagues. Women's fast-pitch was introduced at the [[Summer Olympic Games]] in 1996; softball was excluded in 2024 but returns in 2028. The earliest known game was played in [[Chicago]] on [[Thanksgiving]] Day in 1887. The name "softball" dates to 1926.

Erotic photography, film or other commercial media that is less sexually explicit than [[Hardcore pornography|hardcore]] material. It typically shows nude or semi-nude models in suggestive poses and omits explicit depictions of sexual penetration. Portions considered too graphic may be obscured by hair, clothing, hands or camera angles. Softcore films are commonly less regulated than hardcore and often receive restricted ratings. In [[Germany]], softcore usually receives an FSK-16 rating and hardcore an FSK-18 rating. The boundary with [[Erotica|erotica]] is debated, although erotica is distinguished by high-art standards.

Computer programs and related design documents and specifications. Software is generally divided into [[Operating system|operating systems]], which manage hardware resources and provide services to applications, and [[Application software|application software]], which performs specific tasks for users. The word was first used for computer programs by mathematician John Wilder Tukey in 1958. Early programs were written in machine language until high-level languages such as [[Fortran]], [[Lisp (programming language)|Lisp]] and [[COBOL]] appeared. Software written in a programming language is run through a [[Compiler]] or interpreter. Development involves design, programming, testing, release and maintenance. Under software as a service (SaaS), applications are hosted by a provider and accessed over the [[Internet]], a model enabled by [[Cloud computing]].

Branch of both [[Computer science|computer science]] and [[Engineering|engineering]], concerned with designing, developing, testing and maintaining [[Software|software]] applications. A software engineer applies a development process to define, implement, test, manage and maintain software systems. The discipline was recognized as a separate field from the 1960s, amid a perceived software crisis of over-budget, late projects that required extensive debugging. [[NATO]] organized the first conference on software engineering in 1968. In 1984 the Software Engineering Institute was established at Carnegie Mellon University in [[Pittsburgh]]. Best practices are collected in the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge (SWEBOK). Software is often the primary means of integrating complex system components in modern systems, so the discipline is closely related to systems engineering.

Russian mathematician known for work on analysis, [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] and [[Mechanics|mechanics]]. She was the first woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics in the modern sense, from the University of Göttingen in [[Germany]] in 1874. In 1889 she was appointed to a full professorship in mathematics at the University of [[Stockholm]], the first woman in Europe in modern times to hold such a post. She was also one of the first women to work as an editor for a scientific journal, and she wrote novels and advocated for women's higher education. Historian of science Ann Hibner Koblitz called her "the greatest known woman scientist before the twentieth century."

Ancient Iranian civilization between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers in Central Asia. Its territory corresponds to parts of present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and its city-states, centered on [[Samarkand]], were never politically united. Sogdiana was a province of the [[Achaemenid Empire]], first conquered by [[Cyrus the Great]], and was later annexed by [[Alexander the Great]]. Sogdian, an Eastern Iranian language, was a lingua franca of Central Asia, and Sogdian merchants served as middlemen on the [[Silk Road]]. Sogdians also rose to prominence in the military and government of the [[Tang dynasty]] in China. They practiced [[Zoroastrianism]], [[Manichaeism]] and Buddhism before the Muslim conquest of Transoxiana in the 8th century. Their conversion to Islam was virtually complete by 999, when the Samanid Empire ended.

Ability of a [[Soil|soil]] to sustain agricultural plant growth and consistently yield high-quality crops. A fertile soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts, lacks toxic substances, and has sufficient depth, good drainage, organic matter and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0 for most plants. It also contains [[Microorganism|microorganisms]] that support plant growth. [[Phosphorus]] is the nutrient most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils, and [[Nitrogen]] and [[Potassium]] are also needed in substantial amounts. Inorganic [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]] have higher concentrations of nutrients than organic ones, but their water-soluble [[Nitrate|nitrate]] nitrogen can cause water pollution, while slow-release fertilizers may reduce leaching. Soil erosion and other forms of degradation generally lower fertility, so maintaining it requires conservation practices on agricultural land.

Process of soil genesis, also known as pedogenesis, regulated by the effects of place, environment and history. Biogeochemical processes create and destroy order within soils, forming layers called horizons that differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. Soil forms through [[Weathering|weathering]] of parent material and is influenced by five classic factors: [[Climate|climate]], topography, soil organisms, parent material and time, abbreviated CLORPT. [[Bacteria]] and other microbes feed on nutrients released by weathering and leave organic residues that contribute to humus. In Sicily, under a [[Mediterranean climate]], weathering produces approximately 1/10 mm per year. Most soils form from transported material; wind-blown silt has formed loess soils in the [[Midwestern United States]], while as little as three percent of U.S. soils are residual.

Study of soil as a [[Natural resource|natural resource]] on the Earth's surface, including its [[Soil formation|formation]], classification and mapping. It covers the physical, chemical, biological and [[Soil fertility|fertility]] properties of soils and their management. Its two main branches are pedology, which studies soil in its natural setting, and edaphology, which studies soil in relation to soil-dependent uses. Both draw on soil physics, chemistry and biology, and contributors include engineers, agronomists, geologists and ecologists. The World Reference Base for Soil Resources (WRB) replaced the FAO soil classification as the international system in 1998; its fourth edition dates from 2022. Mapping increasingly uses [[Remote sensing]] to quantify soils in space and time. Research addresses soil's role in [[Climate change]], [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gases]] and carbon sequestration.

American abolitionist and advocate for African American civil rights, [[Women's rights|women's rights]] and temperance. Born into [[Slavery|slavery]] in Swartekill, New York, she escaped with her infant daughter in 1826. In 1828 she won a court case to recover her son, becoming the first Black woman to win such a case against a white man. She took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843. Her best-known speech, delivered extemporaneously at the 1851 Ohio Women's Convention in Akron, became widely known during the Civil War as "Ain't I a Woman?" During the war she helped recruit Black men into the Union army, and afterward she unsuccessfully sought federal land grants for formerly enslaved people. She met [[Abraham Lincoln]] in 1864. In 2009 a memorial bust was unveiled in the U.S. Capitol Visitor Center; she is the first African American woman to have a statue in the Capitol building.

Sunni Muslim caliphate in [[West Africa]], also known as the Sultanate of Sokoto. Founded in 1804 by Usman dan Fodio during the Fulani jihads, after defeating the [[Hausa Kingdoms|Hausa kingdoms]], it covered parts of present-day [[Nigeria]], [[Niger]], [[Cameroon]] and [[Burkina Faso]]. By 1837 it had a population of 10–20 million, the most populous empire in West Africa. It was a loose confederation of emirates recognizing the authority of the sultan of Sokoto, and its scholars produced more than 300 books. By 1900, by one estimate, Sokoto had "at least 1 million and perhaps as many as 2.5 million slaves." The caliphate was dissolved in 1903, when British, French and German forces conquered the area and the last caliph, Attahiru, was killed by British forces.
